summary: Six days after the confession and cross teaching, Jesus is transformed on a mountain before Peter, James, and John. Moses and Elijah appear, but the heavenly voice directs attention to the beloved Son: ‘Listen to him.’ Descending, Jesus connects Elijah's return with John and the Son of Man's suffering. A desperate father meets disciples who cannot heal; Jesus names deficient faith, heals the child, and again predicts betrayal and resurrection. A final temple-tax scene joins Jesus's freedom as Son with a voluntary choice not to cause offense.
whyItMatters: Glory does not cancel the cross; it confirms the person whose suffering teaching disciples must hear. The chapter moves from revelation to ordinary failure and civic-religious obligation, showing authority expressed through listening, dependent faith, compassion, and freely restrained rights.

context.author: Anonymous narrator placing transfiguration after the first passion prediction
context.audience: Disciples tempted to separate glory, power, and freedom from suffering service
context.setting: A high mountain, Galilee, and Capernaum
context.literaryForm: Visionary revelation, healing controversy, passion saying, and distinctive tax anecdote

outline.heading: Transfiguration and the voice: listen to the Son
Failed exorcism, little faith, and mustard seed
Betrayal predicted and temple tax paid freely

keyVerses.text: While he was still speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them. Behold, a voice came out of the cloud, saying, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased. Listen to him.”
keyVerses.why: The baptismal declaration returns with a command that places Jesus above Peter's attempt to manage the scene.

keyVerses.text: He said to them, “Because of your unbelief. For most certainly I tell you, if you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will tell this mountain, ‘Move from here to there,’ and it will move; and nothing will be impossible for you.
keyVerses.why: The smallest seed becomes an image of effective dependence, not heroic quantity of self-confidence.

keyVerses.text: But, lest we cause them to stumble, go to the sea, cast a hook, and take up the first fish that comes up. When you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater coin. Take that, and give it to them for me and you.”
keyVerses.why: Jesus asserts freedom and then voluntarily limits it to avoid an unnecessary obstacle.

questions.question: What does ‘transfigured’ mean?
questions.answer: Metamorphoō means transformed in form or appearance. Matthew describes Jesus's face shining like the sun and clothes becoming light, language of divine glory and apocalyptic revelation. The scene unveils rather than turns Jesus into a different person; the same Son who predicts death is the one revealed in glory.

questions.question: Why Moses and Elijah?
questions.answer: They can represent Law and Prophets, are both associated with Sinai/Horeb revelation, and appear in end-time expectation. Matthew does not state a single reason. The decisive movement is that the cloud's voice names Jesus the beloved Son and, when it clears, the disciples see ‘no one except Jesus alone.’

questions.question: Why are Peter's shelters a mistaken response?
questions.answer: Peter may be extending festival hospitality, trying to preserve the revelation, or placing three figures on a level. Matthew says he speaks before the heavenly interruption but does not call the proposal wicked. The voice redirects him from constructing to listening; revelation cannot be managed as a religious installation.

questions.question: How has Elijah already come?
questions.answer: Jesus identifies John as fulfilling Elijah's preparatory role, not as a claim of reincarnation. John came in prophetic continuity and suffered rejection, which becomes a pattern for the Son of Man. The disciples ‘understood’ the referent after Jesus's explanation.

questions.question: Is the child described with an outdated medical label?
questions.answer: The Greek term is historically linked with being ‘moonstruck,’ and translations vary between epileptic, lunatic, or suffering seizures. The narrative also depicts a demon. Modern readers should neither deny neurological illness nor assume every seizure is spiritual attack; this story reports its own ancient diagnosis and a child's dangerous suffering.

questions.question: Does mustard-seed faith let believers perform any impossible feat?
questions.answer: Jesus addresses disciples who attempted a commissioned act without adequate dependence. The point contrasts tiny real trust with their failure, not faith as a force for achieving every desire. ‘Move mountains’ was a proverbial image for overcoming the impossible; the object remains God's mission and authority.

questions.question: Why is verse 21 missing or footnoted in some Bibles?
questions.answer: A line about prayer and fasting appears in later Matthew manuscripts but is absent from the earliest major Greek witnesses and likely entered from the parallel tradition in Mark. The spiritual practice is biblical elsewhere; the question is whether Matthew originally included this sentence at this location.

questions.question: What is the temple-tax argument about sons and strangers?
questions.answer: Kings tax subjects rather than their own children; Jesus reasons that the Son is free in relation to his Father's temple. Yet he pays ‘lest we cause them to stumble.’ The miraculous provision prevents the scene from becoming mere submission: freedom is real, and it is freely restrained for another's good.

glossary.def: A transformation of visible appearance that reveals Jesus's glory before three disciples.
A coin worth approximately the temple-tax payment for two people in the story.
Greek scandalizō, to cause someone to fall or place a damaging obstacle in the way.
